newsitem.title: UK: Rocky road seen for mining firms after Bre-X.
newsitem.headline: Rocky road seen for mining firms after Bre-X.

text.p: The shockwaves from the Bre-X gold mining scandal will rock the mining sector across the globe for many years to come, analysts said on Tuesday.

Investors' interest in new mining prospects has probably collapsed after a consultant's report on Sunday said claims by Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd for its Busang, Indonesia gold discovery were based on falsified data, they said.
"Basically this has hit the whole mining industry," said Roger Chaplin at stock broker T. Hoare and Company, calling the Bre-X saga a fiasco on an unprecendented scale.

Last weekend mining consultants Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd said its analysis of samples from Busang discovered by the small Calgary-based exploration company Bre-X Minerals contained no gold of economic interest.
According to the Strathcona report, drill core samples from Busang were falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining".
The report meant the end to many investors' dreams after Busang, in the middle of the Indonesian jungle, was labelled as the biggest gold find ever with 71 million ounces of gold reserves.
"I certainly have seen nothing like this ever before," Chaplin said.
In the immediate aftermath of the Bre-X fiasco, many junior mining firms will likely have to postpone any planned fund raising exercises, analysts said.

Some unnamed companies were already rumoured to have cancelled presentations to investors after in March this year due diligence drilling by Busang's putative developer Freeport-McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc showed insigificant amounts of gold at the site.
More "road shows" are likely to be cancelled now that Strathcona has confirmed Freeport's initial findings.
In the long run, mining firms will have to win back investor confidence by putting more time and money into detailed and independent research backing any claims of exciting discoveries.
"The Strathcona report...really is a big downer for the market," said Charles Kernot at Paribas Capital Markets.

He reckons it may take up to five years for people to forget the Bre-X saga, whereas the fall out of previous mining flops took just a couple of months for financial markets to digest. "People will have longish memories (of the Bre-X saga)," he said.
But not all is gloom and doom. The big mining firms may actually benefit and strike co-operation pacts with small exploration firms on more favourable terms than before the Bre-X scandal.
As it will be harder to find money on capital markets, junior companies are likely to be more wiling to join with their big brothers to develop new projects, analysts said.
Equally, with investors shunning small companies, the big firms could take their time and fully use their expertise to assess new mining developments.

The fall out from Bre-X need not be disasterous for London as a centre for raising mining finance, mining equity analysts said, adding that London may become more attractive because it is more tightly regulated than Canadian exchanges.
"London may benefit and detract from Canada as a financing arena," one industry watcher said.
